items.followUp: State the main differences between the five kingdoms in terms of cell type, organization and mode of nutrition.

rubric.why: Gives relevant criteria used to classify organisms into kingdoms.
rubric.description: Names criteria used to establish the five-kingdom classification.
rubric.how: Award for identifying at least two appropriate criteria.

rubric.why: Cell type distinguishes Monera from the other kingdoms.
rubric.description: Distinguishes prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms.
rubric.how: Award for stating that Monera is prokaryotic and the other kingdoms are eukaryotic.

rubric.why: Level of body organization is a basis for separating kingdoms.
rubric.description: Mentions unicellular and multicellular body organization.
rubric.how: Award for correctly referring to both levels of organization.

rubric.why: Mode of nutrition distinguishes major groups such as plants, animals and fungi.
rubric.description: Explains that mode of nutrition is used in classification.
rubric.how: Award for identifying autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition, with a correct example or kingdom distinction.

modelAnswer: R.H. Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom classification using cell structure, body organization, mode of nutrition, reproduction and evolutionary relationships.
Monera consists of prokaryotic organisms; the other four kingdoms consist of eukaryotes.
Organisms may be unicellular or multicellular, and their level of body organization is considered.
Nutrition is also considered: plants are mainly autotrophic, while animals and fungi are heterotrophic.

items.followUp: Define photosynthesis and explain the role of ATP in it.

rubric.why: This captures the definition of bioenergetics.
rubric.description: Defines bioenergetics.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it is the study of energy relationships or transformations in living organisms.

rubric.why: ATP is the molecule that temporarily stores and transfers cellular energy.
rubric.description: Identifies ATP as an energy-carrying molecule.
rubric.how: Award for linking ATP with storage or transfer of energy in cells.

rubric.why: The energy available from ATP is associated with its phosphate bonds.
rubric.description: Explains how ATP stores energy.
rubric.how: Award for identifying energy stored in ATP's phosphate bonds.

rubric.why: ATP releases usable energy when it is converted to ADP and phosphate.
rubric.description: Explains release of energy from ATP.
rubric.how: Award for giving ATP breakdown to ADP and phosphate, with energy released.

rubric.why: ATP is called the energy currency because it supplies energy for cell work.
rubric.description: Explains why ATP is called the cell's energy currency.
rubric.how: Award for stating that ATP transfers usable energy to cellular activities.

modelAnswer: Bioenergetics is the study of energy relationships and energy transformations in living organisms.
ATP (adenosine triphosphate) stores energy in its high-energy phosphate bonds.
When ATP is hydrolysed, it breaks down into ADP and phosphate and releases usable energy.
This energy is transferred to cellular processes that require energy.
ATP is therefore called the cell's energy currency.

items.followUp: Compare rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, giving one function of each.

rubric.why: The ER is a membranous network within the cytoplasm.
rubric.description: Describes the structure of the endoplasmic reticulum.
rubric.how: Award for describing it as a network of membranes, channels, tubes or sacs in the cytoplasm.

rubric.why: Ribosomes attached to the ER give it a rough appearance.
rubric.description: Identifies rough ER and its ribosomes.
rubric.how: Award for correctly stating that rough ER has ribosomes attached.

rubric.why: Ribosomes on rough ER make proteins, which can then be transported.
rubric.description: Gives the function of rough ER.
rubric.how: Award for linking rough ER with protein synthesis or transport.

rubric.why: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and performs functions including lipid synthesis and detoxification.
rubric.description: Identifies a function of smooth ER.
rubric.how: Award for stating a correct smooth ER function, such as lipid synthesis or detoxification.

modelAnswer: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a network of membranes forming channels and sacs throughout the cytoplasm.
Rough ER has ribosomes attached to its surface and is involved in protein synthesis and transport.
Smooth ER has no ribosomes and is involved in lipid synthesis and detoxification.

rubric.why: Parasitology is the branch of biology concerned with parasites.
rubric.description: Defines parasitology.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it studies parasites, including their relationship with hosts.

rubric.why: Entomology is the branch of biology concerned with insects.
rubric.description: Defines entomology.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it studies insects.

modelAnswer: Parasitology is the branch of biology that studies parasites and their relationships with hosts.
Entomology is the branch of biology that studies insects.

items.followUp: What is a colonial organism? Give one example.

rubric.why: Colonial organisms are associated with one another in a group or colony.
rubric.description: States the defining feature of colonial organisms.
rubric.how: Award for saying that individuals live together in a colony or group.

rubric.why: A named colonial organism provides the required example.
rubric.description: Gives an example.
rubric.how: Award for a correct example such as Volvox, Nostoc or Pandorina.

modelAnswer: Colonial organisms are unicellular organisms that live together in a group called a colony.
Example: Volvox.

items.followUp: Give two ways in which scientific theories are tested or supported.

rubric.why: A scientific theory must be supported by observations or experimental evidence.
rubric.description: States that a theory is evidence-based.
rubric.how: Award for referring to observations, experiments or other scientific evidence.

rubric.why: Theories are supported by repeated testing and consistent results.
rubric.description: States that a theory has been repeatedly tested and supported.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a theory has been tested repeatedly or is strongly supported by accumulated evidence.

modelAnswer: A scientific theory is supported by a large amount of evidence from observations and experiments.
It has been repeatedly tested and remains consistent with the available evidence; it can be modified if new evidence requires it.

items.followUp: Explain how water enters a root hair cell by osmosis.

rubric.why: Osmosis allows water to enter plant cells from the surrounding solution.
rubric.description: States that osmosis helps plant cells take up water.
rubric.how: Award for identifying water uptake into plant cells.

rubric.why: Water uptake maintains turgidity and supports the plant; it can also promote cell expansion.
rubric.description: Gives a benefit of water uptake by osmosis.
rubric.how: Award for linking osmosis to turgidity, support or cell expansion.

modelAnswer: Osmosis allows water to enter plant cells through their selectively permeable membranes.
The water makes cells turgid, helping support the plant and allowing cells to expand.

items.followUp: Describe two functions of the large central vacuole in a plant cell.

rubric.why: Vacuoles store water and dissolved substances in the cell sap.
rubric.description: States a storage role of vacuoles.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning storage of water, food or other substances.

rubric.why: The vacuole helps maintain cell turgidity and shape.
rubric.description: States a role in maintaining cell turgidity or shape.
rubric.how: Award for linking the vacuole with turgor pressure, support or maintaining cell shape.

modelAnswer: Vacuoles store water, food and waste materials in the cell sap.
In plant cells, the large central vacuole maintains turgor pressure and helps keep the cell firm.
